column4: Moses’ staff is held to beat foliage down for his sheep; the hand, tree, leaf, and feeding animal give a close Quranic counterpart to the dictionary’s animal reaching up for leaves.
God first draws attention to what Moses holds in his right hand, locating in the hand the staff whose leaf-giving use is explained in 20:18.

Fay is assigned to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so wealth does not merely circulate among the rich; “what the Messenger gives you, take” also makes distribution a commanded giving-and-taking act.
The relative, needy person, and traveler must be given their due without squandering, supplying the right and recipients whose measured delivery continues through 17:29.
Calling squanderers brothers of devils explains one forbidden extreme before 17:29 measures the hand between closure and total extension.
The Lord expands and restricts provision with knowledge, returning the human hand measured in 17:29 to the divine hand that determines its means.
The miserly command others to miserliness and conceal what God gave them from His bounty, opposing both the open hand and the command to make divine favor known.
Those who withhold what God gave them from His bounty will wear the withheld thing as a collar, turning the closed hand into the very bond around the neck evoked by 17:29.
A person vows that if God gives from His bounty he will give charity and become righteous, explicitly promising that the receiving hand will become a giving hand.
Once God gives the promised bounty, the recipient becomes stingy and turns away, breaking the passage of a gift through one hand to another.
God promises to ease the giver of 92:5 toward ease, showing the divine return that follows the praised human gift.
The one who is stingy and imagines himself self-sufficient is the closed-hand reversal of the giver in 92:5.
Being eased toward hardship is the answering outcome of the withholding posture begun in 92:8.
People favored with greater provision refuse to hand it over so that those under their authority might share equally, and the ayah names this refusal a denial of God’s favor.
Joseph’s brothers arrive in hardship with poor merchandise and ask him to give full measure and charity, staging needy petitioners before a powerful hand able to fill theirs.
A wall conceals treasure for two orphan boys until maturity, while God protects their due through an unseen act of mercy rather than allowing a stronger hand to seize it.
The messenger tells Mary he has been sent by her Lord to grant her a pure boy, presenting a divine gift as something brought to its recipient by a messenger.
Whatever believers spend, God replaces it; the giving hand is itself supplied and answered by the supreme Provider.
Believers must spend from that over which God made them successors, showing that the human giver first receives temporary custody from the divine giver.
The command to spend for one’s own good is joined to protection from the soul’s stinginess, identifying the inner force that closes the hand.
The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite their own need, so a needy hand can still open and give rather than treating need as a reason to withhold.
Giving charity secretly to the poor is called better than public disclosure, adding a hidden transfer to the section’s gift that later becomes spoken.
Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, keep the giving hand active across every visible and hidden condition.
Ordinary man becomes withholding when good reaches him, directly opposing the people whose wealth contains the asker’s right in 70:24–25.
If God were to demand all wealth and press people, they would become stingy and expose resentment; the ayah explains the measured divine demand before 47:38 calls them to spend.
The relative, needy person, and traveler must be given their right, making the transfer a due owed to the receiving hand rather than optional largesse.
Sacrificial camels are provision from God from which people must eat and feed both the contented poor and the one who asks, pairing divine gift with two kinds of receiving need.
Israel’s covenant joins good treatment of orphans and the needy with speaking good to people, bringing the beneficent hand and tongue into the same command.
The man is described as one whom God favored and the Prophet also favored, showing divine favor passing through a human relationship rather than ending with its first recipient.
The Prophet is commanded to take charity from believers’ wealth and pray for them; this human taking hand and consoling speech lead directly to God taking charities in 9:104.
Solomon asks his Lord to grant him an incomparable kingdom, supplying the request whose answer is later handed to him as “Our gift” in 38:39.
Immediately after Moses voices need for any good sent down, a woman comes with an invitation to receive a reward for watering, beginning the concrete answer to his open-handed prayer.
After the reminder of divine favor, God promises increase for gratitude and punishment for ingratitude, stating how the recipient’s acknowledgment meets the continuing gift.
The Prophet is commanded to remind people, and the Lord’s favor is named as the reason he is neither soothsayer nor madman; his speech is grounded in received niʿma.
The Lord’s favor is again invoked to reject the charge of madness against the Prophet, giving a specific divine benefit that his proclamation makes known.
Moses and his companion ask a town’s people for food and are refused hospitality, a narrative instance of petitioners being rebuffed.
After rejecting the gift, Solomon sends it back and warns that overpowering armies would expel its senders humbled, showing the gift scene turning toward power from above.
Beside commands to spend, Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty, exposing the rival promises that make a hand close or open.
Those seeking emancipation contracts must be given from the wealth God gave the believers, so an initial divine gift must pass onward to release a dependent person.
Those who are miserly and command others to miserliness are answered by God’s self-sufficiency, another communal spread of the closed-hand posture.
People are told to rejoice in God’s bounty and mercy because it is better than what they accumulate, locating satisfaction in the divine gift rather than in hoarding.
At death a person asks for a short delay in order to give charity, making a would-be giver first an asker before the divine hand that controls time.
Charitable men and women who lend God a good loan receive it multiplied, extending the hand-to-hand loan image to actual donors of charity.
